learn.title: 1 — Congress: Structure, Qualifications & Constitutional Powers (Article I)
learn.body:
Article I of the U.S. Constitution establishes a bicameral national legislature consisting of the House of Representatives and the Senate. The Framers designed differing qualifications and terms to balance democratic responsiveness with institutional stability:

  • House of Representatives: Elected every 2 years; must be at least 25 years old; U.S. citizen for at least 7 years; inhabitant of the state represented.
  • Senate: Elected every 6 years (staggered in 3 classes); must be at least 30 years old; U.S. citizen for at least 9 years; inhabitant of the state represented.

Key Article I, Section 8 Constitutional Powers include:

  • Power of the Purse — Exclusive authority to tax, spend, and borrow money on the credit of the United States.
  • Senate Confirmation Power — Advice and consent on presidential nominations (Cabinet secretaries, ambassadors, and all federal judges, including Supreme Court justices) by majority vote.
  • Impeachment Power — Two-step process: the House holds the sole power to draft and pass articles of impeachment (Resolution to Impeach), while the Senate conducts the trial (conviction requires a 2/3 majority).
  • War & Military Powers — Power to declare war, grant letters of marque and reprisal, and raise/support armies and a navy (Air Force added by statute).
  • Tariff Authority — Congress holds the constitutional power to regulate commerce and levy tariffs, though it delegated emergency tariff authority via statutes like the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 (national security threats).
  • Necessary and Proper Clause (Elastic Clause) — Authority to pass all laws necessary and proper for executing enumerated powers.

learn.title: 2 — Congressional Leadership, Committees & Apportionment
learn.body:
Leadership structures differ sharply between the two chambers:

  • House Leadership: The Speaker of the House (currently Rep. Mike Johnson) is the most powerful officer, elected by the entire House body. The Speaker is the presiding officer, partisan leader of the majority party, and second in line to the presidency (behind the Vice President). Notably, the Constitution does not require the Speaker to be an elected House member. The Speaker appoints committee members/chairs and creates select committees. The House also has a Majority Leader, Minority Leader (Rep. Hakeem Jeffries), and Whips who 'whip up' votes and maintain party discipline.
  • Senate Leadership: The Senate has no Speaker. The constitutional President of the Senate is the Vice President of the United States (JD Vance), who only votes to break ties. Real legislative control rests with the Senate Majority Leader (Sen. John Thune) and Minority Leader (Sen. Chuck Schumer).

Congressional Committees:

  • Standing Committees — Permanent panels that serve as the first stop for proposed bills (e.g., Judiciary, Appropriations).
  • Conference Committees — Temporary ad hoc panels appointed to reconcile differing House and Senate versions of the same bill.
  • Ad Hoc / Select / Special Committees — Temporary committees established for specific investigations or single-issue topics.

Apportionment & Redistricting: House seats are capped at 435 by statute. Every ten years, seats are reapportioned among states using the mathematical equal proportions method based on Decennial Census data. Gerrymandering is the intentional redrawing of district boundaries to favor one party. The last famous mid-decade redistricting solely for political advantage occurred in 2003 (Texas).

learn.title: 3 — Federal Budget, National Debt, Filibuster & Senate Procedure
learn.body:
The federal fiscal year runs from October 1 to September 30. Congress is required to pass 12 separate appropriation bills by September 30 to fully fund the government. If Congress fails to pass these on time, it must enact a Continuing Resolution (CR) — a stopgap spending law that temporarily continues agency funding at existing levels to prevent a government shutdown.

The Senate Filibuster & Nuclear Option:

  • The filibuster allows senators to prolong floor debate to delay or prevent a vote. Under Senate Rule 22, ending debate requires a Cloture vote of 60 votes (three-fifths majority).
  • The Nuclear Option is a procedural maneuver allowing the Senate to alter operating rules by a simple majority (51 votes) rather than a supermajority:
  • 2013 (Democrats): Majority Leader Harry Reid invoked the nuclear option to lower the confirmation threshold to a simple majority for executive branch nominees and lower federal court judges.
  • 2017 (Republicans): Majority Leader Mitch McConnell extended the nuclear option to Supreme Court nominations to confirm Justice Neil Gorsuch.
  • 2019 (Republicans): Used the nuclear option to reduce post-cloture floor debate time for lower-level judicial and executive nominees.

Budget Reconciliation: An expedited parliamentary process created under the 1974 Congressional Budget Act allowing tax, spending, and debt-limit bills to pass the Senate with a simple majority (51 votes), completely bypassing the 60-vote filibuster.

learn.title: 4 — The Executive Branch: Design, Vesting & Powers (Article II)
learn.body:
Article II, Section 1 begins with the Executive Vesting Clause: 'The executive Power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America.' Unlike Article I's enumerated legislative powers, Article II does not explicitly limit executive power in text, creating ongoing constitutional debates over the scope of inherent executive authority.

Executive Design & Electoral College:

  • The President serves a 4-year term, limited to 2 terms by the 22nd Amendment.
  • Qualifications: At least 35 years old, a natural born U.S. citizen, and a resident within the U.S. for at least 14 years.
  • Elected via the Electoral College (538 total votes, 270 to win). 48 states plus Washington D.C. use a winner-take-all system. Only Nebraska and Maine award electoral votes by individual Congressional district, with 2 at-large electoral votes awarded to the statewide winner.

Core Constitutional Powers of the President:

  • Veto Power — Can sign or veto bills passed by Congress; Congress can override a veto with a 2/3 vote in both the House and Senate.
  • Commander-in-Chief — Commands the U.S. Armed Forces, though only Congress can formally declare war.
  • Take Care Clause — Constitutional duty to take care that the laws are faithfully executed.
  • Appointment Power — Appoints ambassadors, Supreme Court and federal judges, and all other officers of the U.S. (interpreted as officers 'exercising significant authority under U.S. laws' like the FBI and DNI) with Senate consent.
  • Treaty & Foreign Policy Powers — Negotiates treaties subject to 2/3 Senate approval; enters into executive agreements.
  • Pardon Power — Unchecked constitutional power to grant reprieves and pardons for federal offenses and treason, but cannot pardon in cases of impeachment.
  • Executive Orders — Unilateral executive directives with the force of law, managing federal operations within statutory and constitutional limits.

learn.title: 5 — Testing Executive Authority: War Powers, Emergencies & Statutory Limits
learn.body:
Modern governance frequently tests the constitutional boundaries of presidential unilateral authority against congressional statutes:

  • War Powers Resolution of 1973 — Enacted over Nixon's veto to curb presidential military action. Requires the President to notify Congress within 48 hours of introducing armed forces into hostilities and mandates troop withdrawal within 60 days (with an optional 30-day extension) unless Congress declares war or authorizes military force. (Debated in modern actions involving Iran).
  • Impoundment Control Act of 1974 — Congress enacted this law to prevent presidents (such as Nixon) from refusing to spend appropriated funds. Because the Constitution dictates that no money can be drawn from the Treasury except via congressional appropriations, presidents cannot unilaterally cancel funds. A 'Pocket Rescission' occurs when a president submits a request to cancel funds so late in a session that Congress cannot act before the funding expires (e.g., USAID funding disputes).
  • Emergency Powers — The President can declare national emergencies under the National Emergencies Act, unlocking statutory emergency authorities.
  • Alien Enemies Act of 1798 — An ancient statutory authority invoked in immigration debates, allowing detention and deportation of noncitizens during declared wars or foreign invasions without standard judicial due process.
  • Domestic Military Deployment — The Posse Comitatus Act of 1878 generally prohibits using federal armed forces for domestic civilian law enforcement. However, the Insurrection Act of 1807 serves as a primary statutory exception, empowering the President to deploy federal troops domestically to suppress insurrections, rebellions, or enforce federal law when states fail to maintain civil order.

learn.title: 6 — The Judicial Branch: Article III & Marbury v. Madison (1803)
learn.body:
Article III, Section 1 vests judicial power in 'one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.' Federal judges hold office 'during good Behaviour' (lifetime tenure unless impeached) and are nominated by the President and confirmed by a Senate majority vote. The Constitution lists no explicit age, citizenship, or law degree requirements for federal judges.

Jurisdiction & the Judiciary Act of 1789:

  • The Judiciary Act of 1789 created the federal court hierarchy: District Courts (federal trial courts) and Circuit Courts (courts of appeals).
  • Original Jurisdiction (SCOTUS hears case first) is explicitly limited by Article III, Section 2 to cases involving ambassadors, public ministers, consuls, and disputes between states.
  • Appellate Jurisdiction covers all other federal cases on appeal from lower federal courts and state supreme courts.

Marbury v. Madison (1803) & Judicial Review:

  • Outgoing Federalist President John Adams appointed 'midnight judges', including William Marbury. Incoming Secretary of State James Madison refused to deliver Marbury's commission.
  • Marbury petitioned the Supreme Court for a Writ of Mandamus (a court order compelling a government official to perform an official duty), citing Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789.
  • Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that while Madison's refusal was illegal, Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional because Congress had improperly expanded the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction beyond what Article III allowed.
  • Marshall established Judicial Review, declaring: 'The constitution is superior to any ordinary act of the legislature... a law repugnant to the constitution is void.'

learn.title: 7 — Judicial Philosophies, Stare Decisis & Landmark Precedents
learn.body:
Judges interpret constitutional text using two primary judicial philosophies:

  • Originalism / Textualism — Interpreting the Constitution according to its original public meaning and text as understood at the time of ratification (favored by conservative jurists like Scalia, Thomas, and Alito).
  • Living Constitution / Evolutionism — Interpreting the Constitution as an evolving document whose meaning adapts to changing societal values and modern circumstances.
  • Stare Decisis — Latin for 'to stand by things decided'; the core legal doctrine requiring judges to respect and adhere to established legal precedents unless compelling justifications warrant overturning them.

Key Recent Landmark Rulings & Doctrines:

  • Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022) — The Court applied an originalist framework to overturn Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey, holding that the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion and returning regulation to the states.
  • West Virginia v. EPA (2022) — Established the Major Questions Doctrine, ruling that regulatory agencies cannot issue rules of vast economic and political significance without explicit, clear statutory authorization from Congress.
  • Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022) — Upheld a high school football coach's right to engage in personal prayer on the 50-yard line, protecting private religious speech under the Free Exercise and Free Speech clauses.
  • Trump v. United States (2024) — Established that former presidents have absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for core constitutional executive acts, presumptive immunity for official acts, and no immunity for unofficial (private) acts.
  • Emergency Docket ('Shadow Docket') — Expedited rulings and emergency orders issued by SCOTUS without regular full briefing, oral argument, or published full opinions (frequently utilized in fast-moving regulatory and election challenges).

learn.title: 8 — Political Parties, Realignment, Georgia Transition & Election Systems
learn.body:
Political Parties & Realignment: Political parties organize to win elections, gain governmental control, and implement public policy by drafting legislation, guiding party votes, nominating candidates, and mobilizing voters. The original two-party division emerged between Federalists (strong central government) and Anti-Federalists / Democratic-Republicans (state autonomy).

A party realignment occurs when long-standing voter coalitions fundamentally shift their allegiance. Modern realignment examples include the Republican MAGA coalition shifting blue-collar/union voters, increases among men of color (Hispanic men from 45% to 54%, Black men from 12% to 20%), and young adult men (35% to 42%). Partisan polarization has led to strict party-line voting, fewer bipartisan moderates, and growing numbers of voters identifying as independents.

Notable Third Parties:

  • Bull Moose (Progressive) Party (1912) — Founded by Teddy Roosevelt; championed campaign finance reform, women's suffrage, social insurance, and the 8-hour workday.
  • Reform Party (1992) — Founded by Ross Perot; focused on eliminating the national debt, campaign finance reform, and congressional term limits.

Georgia Party Realignment Timeline: Georgia was historically a one-party Democratic state from 1872 through 2002. In 2001, Democratic Governor Roy Barnes led a controversial effort to redesign the Georgia state flag (which had featured the Confederate battle emblem since 1956). Backlash from rural conservative voters fractured the Democratic coalition, leading to the historic election of Sonny Perdue in 2002 (took office 2003) as Georgia's first Republican governor since Reconstruction, ushering in two decades of Republican dominance.

Election & Voting Systems:

  • Primary Elections: Closed (only registered party members can vote), Open (voter chooses which primary ballot to cast regardless of registration), Blanket / Jungle (all candidates listed on a single ballot).
  • General Elections: Plurality (most votes wins), Majority (requires >50%; leads to Runoff elections if no one hits 50%, like in Georgia), and Ranked Choice Voting (instant runoff redistribution).

paragraphs.text: The U.S. Constitution designed a bicameral national legislature: a Congress composed of two separate chambers, the Senate and the House of Representatives. Qualification to run for the House of Representatives: elected every two years, at least 25 years old, U.S. citizen for at least seven years, and an inhabitant of the state represented. Qualification for the Senate: elected every six years, at least 30 years old, U.S. citizen for at least nine years, and an inhabitant of the state represented.

Article 1 Constitutional Powers for the Legislative Branch include the power to tax and spend money ('Power of the Purse'), borrow money, establish laws of naturalization, establish lower federal courts, and the Necessary and Proper Clause (Elastic Clause). The Senate holds the confirmation power over presidential nominations (Cabinet and all federal judges including the Supreme Court) by majority vote. The House holds the power to pass a Resolution to Impeach, while the Senate conducts the trial. Congress also possesses the power to declare war, raise an army and navy (with the Air Force added by law), and impose/adjust tariffs under statutes like the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.

Division of labor in Congress: In the House, the Speaker is the most important leadership position, elected by the entire body. The Speaker is the presiding officer and partisan leader of the majority party, and is second in line to the presidency behind the Vice President. The Constitution does not state that the Speaker must be an elected member of the House. Current Speaker: Rep. Mike Johnson. The majority leader holds considerable power; the minority leader is Rep. Hakeem Jeffries; whips enforce party discipline.

In the Senate, there is no Speaker. The Senate's president is the elected Vice President of the United States (JD Vance). Majority and minority leaders hold power: Current Majority Leader Sen. John Thune, Minority Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer. Congressional committees include Standing committees (permanent, first call for proposed bills), Conference committees (ad hoc, reconcile different bills passed in both House and Senate), and Ad hoc/Select committees (temporary, conduct special investigations). Gerrymandering is the manipulative dividing of election district boundaries. Apportionment uses the equal proportions method based on Decennial Census data every ten years, capping House seats at 435. The last notable mid-decade redistricting for political reasons occurred in 2003 in Texas.

The federal budget must be passed by September 30 across 12 Appropriation Bills. The budget year runs from October 1 to September 30. If appropriations are not enacted on time, Congress passes a Continuing Resolution to avoid shutdowns. In the Senate, the Filibuster allows prolonged debate, requiring Cloture (60 votes) to end. The Nuclear Option was invoked in 2013 by Senate Democrats led by Harry Reid to lower the threshold to a simple majority for executive branch and lower federal judges. In 2017, Senate Republicans extended the nuclear option to Supreme Court nominations for Neil Gorsuch, and in 2019 used it to reduce debate time. Budget Reconciliation allows certain budget, tax, and debt limit bills to pass with a simple majority (51 votes).

Article II, Section 1 vests executive power in a single President elected by the Electoral College for a four-year term, limited to two terms. Qualifications: at least thirty-five years old, natural born U.S. citizen, and fourteen years an inhabitant of the U.S. Electoral votes are winner-take-all except in Nebraska and Maine, which award votes by Congressional district. Presidential powers include vetoing bills (overridden by 2/3 vote in both chambers), Commander-in-Chief, executing laws faithfully, appointment of officers and judges with Senate confirmation, making treaties (2/3 Senate approval), pardons (federal cases and treason, but not impeachment), and issuing executive orders.

Limits on executive power include the War Powers Resolution of 1973 (notification within 48 hours, 60-day limit without Congressional authorization) and the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which prevents the President from refusing to spend congressionally appropriated funds ('Power of the Purse' — 'No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law'). Pocket rescissions occur when cancellation requests are submitted too late for Congress to act. The Alien Enemies Act of 1798 grants emergency deportation powers during foreign conflict. Domestic military deployment is restricted by the Posse Comitatus Act of 1878, but permitted under the Insurrection Act of 1807 to suppress rebellion.

Article III vests judicial power in one Supreme Court and inferior courts established by Congress. Justices hold office 'during good Behaviour' (lifetime tenure unless impeached) and are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate by majority vote. The Judiciary Act of 1789 created District Courts and Circuit Courts. Section 2 of Article III defines original jurisdiction (ambassadors, public ministers, consuls, and disputes between states). In Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that Congress's expansion of original jurisdiction via Section 13 of the 1789 Act was unconstitutional, establishing Judicial Review: 'a law repugnant to the constitution is void.'

Judicial interpretation features distinct philosophies: Originalists (framers' intent and original text meaning) versus Living Constitution / Evolutionists (adapting to modern society). Stare Decisis is the legal principle of determining litigation according to precedent ('stand by things decided'). Recent cases include West Virginia v. EPA (Major Questions Doctrine), Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (prayer rights), Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (overturning Roe v. Wade), and Trump v. United States (presidential immunity for official acts). The Court also uses the Emergency 'Shadow' Docket for rapid orders without full briefing.

Political parties work to win elections and implement policy by drafting legislation, guiding party voting, nominating candidates, and mobilizing voters. Party realignment occurs when voter coalitions shift, such as modern shifts among blue-collar workers, young adults, and men of color toward the Republican MAGA movement. Partisan polarization has reduced split-ticket voting and expanded independent voters. Notable third parties include Teddy Roosevelt's Bull Moose Party (1912; suffrage, social insurance, 8-hour workday) and Ross Perot's Reform Party (1992; debt reduction, term limits). In Georgia, Democratic Governor Roy Barnes changed the state flag in 2001, alienating rural conservative Democrats and leading to Sonny Perdue's historic election in 2002 (taking office 2003) as the first Republican governor since Reconstruction. Election systems include open, closed, and blanket primaries, as well as plurality, majority (runoffs), and ranked choice voting in general elections.

anki.q: What are the constitutional age and citizenship requirements for the House of Representatives?
anki.a: Must be at least 25 years old and a U.S. citizen for at least 7 years (and an inhabitant of the state represented). Elected every 2 years.

anki.q: What are the constitutional age and citizenship requirements for the Senate?
anki.a: Must be at least 30 years old and a U.S. citizen for at least 9 years (and an inhabitant of the state represented). Elected every 6 years.

anki.q: What is the constitutional process and required vote for impeachment?
anki.a: The House of Representatives passes a Resolution/Articles of Impeachment by a simple majority; the Senate conducts the trial and requires a 2/3 majority vote to convict and remove from office.

anki.q: What vote fraction is required in Congress to override a presidential veto?
anki.a: A 2/3 supermajority vote in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

anki.q: Does the U.S. Constitution require the Speaker of the House to be an elected member of Congress?
anki.a: No. The Constitution does not state that the Speaker must be an elected member of the House, though every Speaker in history has been one.

anki.q: Who is second in the presidential line of succession behind the Vice President?
anki.a: The Speaker of the House.

anki.q: What is the difference between Standing, Conference, and Select/Ad Hoc committees?
anki.a: Standing committees are permanent (first stop for bills); Conference committees are temporary ad hoc panels to reconcile House and Senate versions of a bill; Select/Ad Hoc committees are temporary panels created for specific investigations or single issues.

anki.q: What is gerrymandering, and what method is used for congressional seat reapportionment?
anki.a: Gerrymandering is the manipulative redrawing of legislative district boundaries to favor one party. Apportionment uses the mathematical 'equal proportions method' based on Decennial Census data every 10 years (House capped at 435 seats).

anki.q: When does the federal fiscal year begin and end, and what is a Continuing Resolution (CR)?
anki.a: The fiscal year runs from October 1 to September 30 (12 appropriation bills required). A Continuing Resolution is a temporary stopgap spending bill that funds government agencies at current levels to prevent a shutdown.

anki.q: What is a filibuster and what vote is required for Cloture in the Senate?
anki.a: A filibuster is an effort to extend Senate debate to block or delay a vote. Cloture (Senate Rule 22) requires 60 votes (three-fifths of the Senate) to end debate on legislation.

anki.q: Explain the history of the Senate 'Nuclear Option' in 2013 and 2017.
anki.a: In 2013, Senate Democrats (Harry Reid) lowered the threshold to a simple majority (51 votes) for executive nominees and lower federal judges. In 2017, Senate Republicans extended it to Supreme Court nominations (Neil Gorsuch).

anki.q: What is Budget Reconciliation and why is it strategically important in the Senate?
anki.a: A legislative procedure created by the 1974 Congressional Budget Act that allows tax, spending, and debt-limit bills to pass the Senate with a simple majority (51 votes), immune to the 60-vote filibuster.

anki.q: What are the constitutional qualifications to serve as President of the United States?
anki.a: Must be at least 35 years old, a natural-born U.S. citizen, and a resident within the United States for at least 14 years (Article II, Section 1).

anki.q: Which two states do not use a winner-take-all Electoral College system?
anki.a: Maine and Nebraska (they award electoral votes by individual Congressional district, plus 2 at-large votes for the statewide winner).

anki.q: What are the core requirements and time limits of the War Powers Resolution of 1973?
anki.a: The President must notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying troops into hostilities and must withdraw forces within 60 days unless Congress explicitly authorizes military force or declares war.

anki.q: What is the Impoundment Control Act of 1974 and what constitutional clause does it defend?
anki.a: It forbids the President from refusing to spend congressionally appropriated funds without congressional approval. It enforces Article I's 'Power of the Purse' ('No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law').

anki.q: What are the limits on the President's constitutional pardon power?
anki.a: The President can only pardon federal offenses (including treason), and cannot pardon in cases of impeachment or for state-level criminal convictions.

anki.q: What is the difference between the Posse Comitatus Act of 1878 and the Insurrection Act of 1807?
anki.a: Posse Comitatus (1878) strictly prohibits using federal military troops for domestic civilian law enforcement. The Insurrection Act (1807) provides the major exception, allowing the President to deploy troops domestically to suppress rebellions or enforce federal law.

anki.q: What is the Alien Enemies Act of 1798?
anki.a: A wartime statute that allows the President to detain and deport noncitizens from hostile foreign nations during declared wars or invasions without standard judicial due process.

anki.q: What are the constitutional qualifications and term lengths for federal judges under Article III?
anki.a: There are no constitutional age, citizenship, or legal degree requirements. Federal judges hold office 'during good Behaviour' (lifetime tenure unless impeached) and are confirmed by a simple majority in the Senate.

anki.q: What court levels were established by the Judiciary Act of 1789?
anki.a: District Courts (federal trial courts), Circuit Courts (courts of appeals), and the structure of the Supreme Court.

anki.q: What cases fall under the Supreme Court's Original Jurisdiction according to Article III, Section 2?
anki.a: Cases involving Ambassadors, public ministers, consuls, and controversies in which a U.S. State is a party.

anki.q: What was the core holding and significance of Marbury v. Madison (1803)?
anki.a: Chief Justice John Marshall established Judicial Review. The Court held that Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional because Congress cannot expand SCOTUS original jurisdiction beyond Article III. 'A law repugnant to the constitution is void.'

anki.q: What is a 'Writ of Mandamus'?
anki.a: A court order commanding a government official to perform a mandatory, nondiscretionary public or official duty (the remedy William Marbury sought against James Madison).

anki.q: Compare Originalism with Living Constitution (Evolutionism).
anki.a: Originalism interprets constitutional text according to its original public meaning at the time of adoption. Living Constitution (Evolutionism) interprets the Constitution as an evolving document whose meaning adapts to changing societal values and modern circumstances.

anki.q: What does the Latin term 'Stare Decisis' mean in constitutional law?
anki.a: Literally 'to stand by things decided'; the legal doctrine that courts must adhere to established judicial precedents in subsequent cases.

anki.q: What was the ruling in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022)?
anki.a: The Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey, holding that the U.S. Constitution does not confer a right to abortion, returning regulatory authority entirely to the states.

anki.q: What doctrine was established in West Virginia v. EPA (2022)?
anki.a: The Major Questions Doctrine, holding that executive and regulatory agencies cannot issue regulations of vast economic and political significance without explicit, clear statutory authorization from Congress.

anki.q: What did the Supreme Court rule in Trump v. United States (2024)?
anki.a: Presidents have absolute immunity for core constitutional executive acts, presumptive immunity for official acts within the outer perimeter of responsibility, and no immunity for unofficial (private) acts.

anki.q: What is the Supreme Court's Emergency Docket ('Shadow Docket')?
anki.a: The Court's process for issuing emergency rulings, stays, and injunctions on expedited timelines without full briefing, oral arguments, or detailed published opinions.

anki.q: What were the platform goals of Teddy Roosevelt's Bull Moose (Progressive) Party in 1912?
anki.a: Campaign finance reform, women's suffrage, social insurance, and the 8-hour workday.

anki.q: What were the key platform issues of Ross Perot's Reform Party in 1992?
anki.a: Reducing the federal national debt, campaign finance reform, and congressional term limits (Perot won ~19% of the popular vote).

anki.q: What catalytic event triggered Georgia's party realignment in 2001–2003?
anki.a: In 2001, Democratic Governor Roy Barnes led the effort to remove the prominent Confederate battle emblem from the Georgia state flag. Backlash alienated conservative rural voters, leading to Sonny Perdue's 2002 election as the first Republican governor since Reconstruction.

anki.q: What is the difference between Closed, Open, and Blanket/Jungle primaries?
anki.a: Closed: only registered party members can vote in that party's primary. Open: any registered voter can choose which primary ballot to cast. Blanket/Jungle: all candidates from all parties appear on one ballot, and top vote-getters advance regardless of party.

anki.q: What is the difference between Plurality and Majority voting systems?
anki.a: Plurality (First-Past-The-Post): the candidate with the most votes wins, even if under 50%. Majority: the winning candidate must secure over 50% of the vote (triggering a runoff between top two finishers if no candidate reaches 50%, as in Georgia).

anki.q: What is Ranked Choice Voting (Instant Runoff)?
anki.a: A voting system where voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins a majority of first-place votes, the lowest candidate is eliminated and their votes are redistributed until one candidate secures a majority.

anki.q: Who are the current congressional party leaders in the House and Senate?
anki.a: House: Speaker Mike Johnson (R), Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D). Senate: Majority Leader John Thune (R), Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D), President of Senate JD Vance (VP).

anki.q: What was the significance of the 2003 Texas mid-decade redistricting?
anki.a: Led by Tom DeLay, Texas redrew congressional district lines mid-decade solely for partisan gain rather than waiting for the decennial census, a tactic upheld by the Supreme Court in LULAC v. Perry.

anki.q: What is the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 (Section 232)?
anki.a: A federal law authorizing the President to impose or adjust tariffs on imported goods if the Department of Commerce determines those imports threaten U.S. national security.

anki.q: What are the rules and logistics announced for the in-class Midterm 2 exam?
anki.a: In-class exam (ends 12:15 PM), closed-book/no notes, attendance mandatory, strictly forbidden from leaving Canvas browser (results in zero), and grades shown immediately upon completion (missed questions hidden until all students complete test).

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly pairs the congressional chamber with its constitutional age and citizenship requirements?
options: House: 21 years old, 5 years citizen; Senate: 30 years old, 9 years citizen
House: 25 years old, 7 years citizen; Senate: 30 years old, 9 years citizen
House: 25 years old, 9 years citizen; Senate: 35 years old, 14 years citizen
House: 30 years old, 7 years citizen; Senate: 35 years old, 9 years citizen
quiz.explanation: Article I requires House members to be at least 25 years old and citizens for 7 years, while Senators must be at least 30 years old and citizens for 9 years.

quiz.q: Under the U.S. Constitution, which chamber of Congress holds the power to impeach, and which holds the power to conduct the trial and convict?
options: Senate impeaches by simple majority; House conducts trial by 2/3 majority
House impeaches by simple majority; Supreme Court conducts trial by unanimous vote
House impeaches by simple majority; Senate conducts trial by 2/3 majority
House and Senate must jointly pass an impeachment resolution by 2/3 majority
quiz.explanation: The House of Representatives has the sole power of impeachment (passing the resolution/articles), and the Senate has the sole power to try all impeachments, requiring a 2/3 vote to convict.

quiz.q: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), why did Chief Justice John Marshall strike down Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789?
options: Because Thomas Jefferson had the absolute power to cancel all previous judicial appointments
Because Congress unconstitutionally expanded the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction beyond Article III
Because William Marbury was not qualified to serve as a justice of the peace under the Constitution
Because the President cannot appoint judges without the prior consent of the House of Representatives
quiz.explanation: Marshall ruled that Section 13 of the 1789 Act unconstitutionally gave SCOTUS the original jurisdiction to issue writs of mandamus directly to executive officials, exceeding the strict original jurisdiction limits set by Article III, Section 2.

quiz.q: What is the primary statutory difference between the Posse Comitatus Act of 1878 and the Insurrection Act of 1807 regarding military deployment on domestic soil?
options: Posse Comitatus allows military policing; Insurrection Act strictly forbids all domestic troop deployment
Posse Comitatus prohibits federal troops from civilian law enforcement; Insurrection Act is a major statutory exception allowing deployment to suppress rebellions
Posse Comitatus applies only to the Navy; Insurrection Act applies only to the Army and National Guard
Both acts were declared unconstitutional in Trump v. United States (2024)
quiz.explanation: The Posse Comitatus Act (1878) prohibits federal military personnel from acting as civilian domestic police, while the Insurrection Act (1807) provides the explicit presidential exception to deploy troops to suppress domestic violence or enforce federal law.

quiz.q: Under the War Powers Resolution of 1973, what are the President's obligations when deploying armed forces into hostile situations without a declaration of war?
options: Notify Congress within 24 hours; withdraw troops within 30 days unless Congress ratifies a treaty
Notify Congress within 48 hours; withdraw troops within 60 days unless Congress authorizes force or declares war
Notify the Supreme Court within 48 hours; obtain written permission from the Speaker of the House within 90 days
Obtain unanimous consent from the Senate Armed Services Committee prior to any troop movement
quiz.explanation: The War Powers Resolution requires presidential notification to Congress within 48 hours of troop deployment into hostilities and mandates withdrawal within 60 days unless Congress grants authorization.

quiz.q: In the Senate, what procedural threshold is required to invoke Cloture under Rule 22 to end a filibuster on regular legislation?
options: A simple majority of 51 votes
Three-fifths of all sworn senators (60 votes)
Two-thirds of senators present and voting (67 votes)
Three-fourths of state delegations
quiz.explanation: Ending a Senate filibuster on legislation requires a Cloture vote under Rule 22, requiring three-fifths of all senators (60 votes).

quiz.q: What landmark event in 2001 catalysed the dramatic political party transition in Georgia from Democratic to Republican control?
options: Sonny Perdue switched parties from Democrat to Republican during his Senate term
Democratic Governor Roy Barnes led the controversial legislative effort to change the Georgia state flag
The Supreme Court mandated mid-decade redistricting across all southern congressional districts
The Georgia General Assembly adopted Ranked Choice Voting for all statewide elections
quiz.explanation: In 2001, Democratic Governor Roy Barnes led the change of Georgia's state flag to diminish the Confederate battle cross, causing severe rural backlash that swept Republican Sonny Perdue into the governor's mansion in 2002/2003.

quiz.q: Which of the following presidential pardon limitations is explicitly stated in Article II, Section 2 of the Constitution?
options: The President cannot pardon individuals convicted of treason
The President cannot grant pardons in cases of impeachment
The President must obtain majority approval from the Senate Judiciary Committee for any pardon
The President can only issue pardons during their second term in office
quiz.explanation: Article II, Section 2 grants the President power to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, 'except in Cases of Impeachment.'

quiz.q: What does the Latin legal doctrine 'Stare Decisis' require of judicial decision-making?
options: Judges must defer entirely to executive orders issued by the sitting President
Courts must adhere to established legal precedents when resolving similar litigation
All judicial opinions must be grounded strictly in the 1787 Federalist Papers
Federal courts must yield jurisdiction to state supreme courts in civil disputes
quiz.explanation: Stare Decisis literally translates to 'to stand by things decided' and represents the fundamental legal doctrine that courts should follow established judicial precedent.

quiz.q: Which major statutory rule was created by the Impoundment Control Act of 1974?
options: The President is prohibited from unilaterally refusing to spend funds appropriated by Congress
Congress must pass all 12 appropriation bills as a single omnibus package by December 31
The President can permanently cancel any line-item appropriation using executive orders
Federal agencies must maintain a balanced budget without using Continuing Resolutions
quiz.explanation: The Impoundment Control Act of 1974 curtailed presidential impoundment, requiring the President to spend congressionally appropriated funds unless Congress explicitly approves a deferral or rescission.
